questions.stem: Which list contains only strong acids?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acid ionise almost completely in water. Carboxylic acids such as ethanoic and citric acid, and carbonic acid, are weak acids that ionise only partly.

questions.stem: Which substance is a strong base?
questions.explanation: Group 1 hydroxides and barium hydroxide dissociate completely in water, so they are strong bases. Ammonia and amines such as methylamine react only partly with water, so they are weak bases.

questions.stem: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, can donate three protons per molecule. It is described as:
questions.explanation: An acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule is polyprotic; H₃PO₄ is triprotic. Amphiprotic describes a species that can either donate or accept a proton.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has four hydrogen atoms but is monoprotic. Why?
options: Three of its hydrogen atoms are lost as hydrogen gas in water
It is a weak acid, so it can only ever donate one proton
The hydrogen atoms on carbon are donated only to strong bases
Only the hydrogen in the -COOH group is released as a proton
questions.explanation: Only the hydrogen bonded to oxygen in the carboxyl group is polar enough to be donated in water. The three hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not acidic. Being weak is about the extent of ionisation, not the number of protons.

questions.stem: A solution of 0.001 M hydrochloric acid is best described as:
questions.explanation: Strength describes the extent of ionisation: HCl ionises completely, so it is strong. Concentration describes the amount of acid per litre: 0.001 M is dilute.

questions.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid, each 0.10 M, are compared at 25 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: The hydrochloric acid has the higher pH but the higher conductivity
The hydrochloric acid has the lower pH and the higher electrical conductivity
The ethanoic acid has the lower pH and the higher electrical conductivity
Both have the same pH, because they have the same concentration
questions.explanation: HCl ionises completely, giving [H⁺] = 0.10 M and many ions, while ethanoic acid ionises only slightly. The HCl therefore has the higher [H⁺], the lower pH and the higher conductivity, although the concentrations of acid are equal.

questions.stem: Equal masses of magnesium ribbon are added to 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl and to 50 mL of 1.0 M CH₃COOH. The acid is in excess in both. Which statement is correct?
options: Both react at the same rate, because the acid concentrations are equal
CH₃COOH reacts faster, because it has more hydrogen atoms per molecule
HCl reacts faster, but both produce the same total volume of hydrogen
HCl reacts faster and produces a greater total volume of hydrogen
questions.explanation: The higher [H⁺] in the strong acid makes collisions with H⁺ more frequent, so the rate is higher. The magnesium is limiting, so the total amount of hydrogen depends only on the mass of magnesium; as H⁺ is used up, more ethanoic acid ionises.

questions.stem: Water is a weak electrolyte because:
options: it contains no ions at all at 25 °C
it ionises completely into H⁺ and OH⁻
its molecules carry an overall charge
questions.explanation: Water self-ionises slightly, H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), giving Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. The very low ion concentrations mean pure water conducts electricity only very poorly.

questions.stem: A solution at 25 °C has [OH⁻] = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M. What is [H⁺]?
questions.explanation: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 5.0 × 10⁻¹² M. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ M.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0050 M nitric acid at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid is a strong monoprotic acid, so [H⁺] = 0.0050 M and pH = −log₁₀(0.0050) = 2.30. The value 11.70 is the pOH.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.020 M barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Each Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH⁻ ions, so [OH⁻] = 0.040 M and pOH = −log₁₀(0.040) = 1.40. Then pH = 14.00 − 1.40 = 12.60. Ignoring the 2 gives 12.30, and 1.40 is the pOH, not the pH.

questions.stem: A sodium hydroxide solution has a pH of 12.0 at 25 °C. What is its concentration?
questions.explanation: pOH = 14.0 − 12.0 = 2.0, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻² M, and NaOH is a strong base with one OH⁻ per formula unit. The value 1.0 × 10⁻¹² M is [H⁺].

questions.stem: In the Brønsted-Lowry model, a base is a substance that:
options: accepts a pair of electrons from water
questions.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors. Releasing hydroxide ions describes a base in the older Arrhenius model, which cannot explain bases such as ammonia that contain no hydroxide.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: A conjugate base has one fewer H⁺ than its acid, so removing one proton from H₂PO₄⁻ gives HPO₄²⁻, with the charge lowered by one. H₃PO₄ is its conjugate acid.

questions.stem: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which pair is a conjugate acid-base pair?
questions.explanation: A conjugate pair differs by a single proton. HCO₃⁻ donates a proton to become CO₃²⁻; the other pair is H₃O⁺ and H₂O. HCO₃⁻ and H₂O are the two reactants, acid and base, not a conjugate pair.

questions.stem: Which species is amphiprotic?
questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ can donate a proton to become SO₄²⁻ or accept one to become H₂SO₄, so it can act as an acid or a base. SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻ have no proton to donate, and NH₄⁺ cannot accept another proton.

questions.stem: Methylamine is a weak base. Which equation shows its reaction with water?
questions.explanation: Like ammonia, the amine accepts a proton from water, forming CH₃NH₃⁺ and OH⁻. It is weak, so the reaction is an equilibrium (⇌) that lies to the left; a one-way arrow would imply complete reaction.

questions.stem: A buffer solution is best described as:
options: a solution of a strong acid that keeps its pH low when diluted
a neutral salt solution that does not react with acids or bases
a solution whose pH changes sharply when a base is added
a solution of a conjugate acid-base pair that resists changes in pH
questions.explanation: A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in similar amounts, so it can react with small amounts of added acid or base and resist a change in pH.

questions.stem: A buffer contains ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate: CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq). A small amount of HCl is added. Which explanation is correct?
options: The added Cl⁻ ions react with H⁺, so [H⁺] returns to its original value
The equilibrium does not shift, because the buffer contains no OH⁻
The equilibrium shifts left, as CH₃COO⁻ reacts with most of the added H⁺
The equilibrium shifts right, as CH₃COOH ionises to replace the H⁺
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle, added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left: ethanoate ions combine with most of the extra H⁺ to form ethanoic acid. [H⁺] rises only slightly, so the pH barely changes. Chloride is a spectator ion.

questions.stem: For hydrofluoric acid, HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq), the expression for Ka is:
questions.explanation: Ka is products over reactants, with water omitted because, as the solvent, its concentration is effectively constant. Leaving out [HF] would make it the expression for an ionic product, not Ka.

questions.stem: Four weak acids have the pKa values below. Which is the strongest acid? Methanoic 3.75, ethanoic 4.76, benzoic 4.20, propanoic 4.87.
questions.explanation: pKa = −log₁₀Ka, so the smallest pKa corresponds to the largest Ka and the greatest degree of ionisation. Methanoic acid, with pKa 3.75, is the strongest of the four; propanoic acid, with the largest pKa, is the weakest.

questions.stem: What is the pKa of an acid with Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵?
questions.explanation: pKa = −log₁₀(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 4.74. The value 9.26 is the pKb of its conjugate base, since pKa + pKb = 14.00 at 25 °C.

questions.stem: A 0.10 M solution of ethanoic acid has a pH of 2.88. What is Ka for ethanoic acid? Assume [CH₃COOH] at equilibrium is 0.10 M.
A weak acid HA has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of a 0.10 M solution? State any assumption.
options: 1.00, assuming HA is completely ionised in water
questions.explanation: Ka = [H⁺]²/[HA]. Because Ka is small, assume [HA] ≈ 0.10 M, so [H⁺]² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶, [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M and pH = 3.00. Treating the weak acid as fully ionised gives 1.00.

questions.stem: The ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, has Ka = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is Kb for ammonia, NH₃?
questions.explanation: For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, so Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Multiplying Ka by Kw instead gives the tiny value 5.6 × 10⁻²⁴.

questions.stem: A 0.10 M weak acid solution has [H⁺] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ M. What percentage of the acid molecules have ionised?
questions.explanation: Percentage ionisation = [H⁺]/[HA]initial × 100 = (1.3 × 10⁻³ / 0.10) × 100 = 1.3%. A low degree of ionisation is what makes the acid weak.

questions.stem: A 0.10 M solution of a strong acid and a 0.10 M solution of a weak acid are each diluted tenfold. How do their pH values change?
options: Both pH values fall, because the acid molecules are more spread out
The strong acid's pH rises by 1; the weak acid's pH rises by less than 1
Both pH values rise by exactly 1, because both are diluted tenfold
The weak acid's pH rises by 1; the strong acid's pH rises by less than 1
questions.explanation: For the strong acid, [H⁺] falls tenfold, so pH rises by exactly 1. For the weak acid, dilution shifts its ionisation equilibrium to the right, so [H⁺] falls by less than a factor of 10 and pH rises by less than 1 (about 0.5).

questions.stem: An acid-base indicator HIn(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + In⁻(aq) changes colour when:
questions.explanation: At pH = pKa, [HIn] = [In⁻], so the solution shows the intermediate colour. Each indicator changes colour at its own pH, which is why indicators must be matched to the titration.

questions.stem: An indicator is a weak acid HIn. Its acid form HIn is yellow and its base form In⁻ is blue. What colour is it in a strongly acidic solution, and why?
options: Yellow, because In⁻ reacts with water to form OH⁻ ions
Yellow, because high [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the left
Blue, because high [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium to the right
Green, because both coloured forms are always present equally
questions.explanation: Added H⁺ shifts HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ to the left, so the yellow HIn form dominates. In a basic solution OH⁻ removes H⁺, the equilibrium shifts right and the blue In⁻ form dominates.

questions.stem: The end point of a titration is:
options: the point at which the reactants are in stoichiometric ratio
the point at which the pH of the mixture is exactly 7
the point at which half of the analyte has reacted
the point at which the indicator changes colour
questions.explanation: The end point is observed when the indicator changes colour. The equivalence point is when the reactants have been mixed in the mole ratio of the equation; a well-chosen indicator makes the two very close.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide; the equivalence point is at pH 8.7. Which indicator, with pKa shown, is most suitable? Assume each changes colour over pKa ± 1. P: 3.7, Q: 5.0, R: 7.1, S: 9.3.
questions.explanation: The indicator's range must include the equivalence point pH. S changes over about 8.3 to 10.3, which contains 8.7. R changes over about 6.1 to 8.1, so it would change before the equivalence point and give a low titre.

questions.stem: Compared with the titration curve of a strong acid with a strong base, the curve for a weak acid with a strong base has:
options: the same starting pH and a longer vertical section around pH 7
a higher starting pH and an equivalence point at exactly pH 7
a higher starting pH, a buffer region and an equivalence point above pH 7
a lower starting pH, a buffer region and an equivalence point below pH 7
questions.explanation: The weak acid is only partly ionised, so it starts at a higher pH. It forms a buffer with its conjugate base before equivalence, and at equivalence the conjugate base makes the solution basic, so the equivalence point is above pH 7.

questions.stem: Ammonia solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid. At the equivalence point the solution is:
options: basic, because excess NH₃ remains in the flask
neutral, because a salt and water have formed
basic, because Cl⁻ ions accept protons from water
acidic, because NH₄⁺ ions donate protons to water
questions.explanation: At equivalence the flask contains NH₄Cl. NH₄⁺ is a weak acid that donates protons to water, so the pH is below 7. Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not affect the pH.

questions.stem: A weak acid is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. The equivalence point is at 25.0 mL, and the pH after 12.5 mL is 4.8. What is Ka for the acid?
questions.explanation: At half the equivalence volume, half the acid has become its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa = 4.8. Ka = 10^(−4.8) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵. The value 6.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ is Kb for the conjugate base.

questions.stem: 25.00 mL of sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with 0.100 M HCl. The average titre is 20.00 mL. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.02000 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol, which equals n(NaOH) in the 1:1 reaction. c(NaOH) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.02500 = 0.0800 M. Swapping the two volumes gives 0.125 M.

questions.stem: 18.00 mL of 0.0500 M H₂SO₄ exactly neutralises 25.00 mL of NaOH solution. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0500 × 0.01800 = 9.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, so n(NaOH) = 1.80 × 10⁻³ mol and c = 1.80 × 10⁻³ / 0.02500 = 0.0720 M. Treating the ratio as 1:1 gives 0.0360 M.

questions.stem: 1.325 g of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (M = 105.99 g/mol) is made up to 250.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot needs 22.50 mL of HCl to reach the end point: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is c(HCl)?
questions.explanation: c(Na₂CO₃) = (1.325/105.99)/0.2500 = 0.05000 M, so the aliquot holds 1.000 × 10⁻³ mol and needs 2.000 × 10⁻³ mol of HCl. c(HCl) = 2.000 × 10⁻³ / 0.02250 = 0.0889 M. Forgetting the 2:1 ratio gives 0.0444 M.

questions.stem: In a conductometric titration of 20.0 mL of HCl with 0.100 M NaOH, the conductivity reaches a minimum at 15.0 mL of NaOH. What is the concentration of the HCl?
questions.explanation: The minimum marks the equivalence point. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0150 = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl), so c(HCl) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.0200 = 0.0750 M. Swapping the volumes gives 0.133 M.

questions.stem: During the conductometric titration of HCl with NaOH, why does the conductivity fall before the equivalence point and rise after it?
options: Highly mobile H⁺ ions are replaced by slower Na⁺ ions, then excess OH⁻ and Na⁺ accumulate
The number of ions falls to zero at equivalence, then rises as water ionises
Na⁺ ions are more mobile than H⁺ ions, so the conductivity falls until all Na⁺ reacts
Water molecules conduct electricity, and their number falls and then rises again
questions.explanation: Before equivalence each H⁺ that reacts with OH⁻ is replaced by an Na⁺ ion, which conducts far less well than H⁺, so conductivity falls. After equivalence excess OH⁻ (also highly mobile) and Na⁺ ions build up, so it rises. Ions are still present at equivalence.

questions.stem: Carborane acids are among the strongest known acids. What property of the carborane anion helps make them so strong?
options: It contains many hydroxide groups that release OH⁻
It is a very strong base that accepts protons readily
It is very stable and an extremely weak base
It forms strong bonds that hold the proton tightly
questions.explanation: An acid is strong when its conjugate base has little tendency to take back the proton. The carborane anion is exceptionally stable and unreactive, so it is an extremely weak base and the proton is given up very readily.
